newsitem.title: USA: Sears one of several retailers under investigation.
newsitem.headline: Sears one of several retailers under investigation.

text.p: Sears, Roebuck & Co., which has agreed to pay $165 million for wrongly trying to collect credit card debts, is only one of several retailers under investigation for the practice, officials said Friday.
Officials from 40 states that have targeted Sears are now turning their focus on other retailers, an official at the Massachusetts Attorney General's office said.

"We are planning on looking at other retailers," said George Weber, head of consumer affairs in the state Attorney General's office. "The multistate group will continue. This is the most significant coordination effort ever undertaken by the attorneys general."

Sears agreed on Thursday to pay $40 million to the states and at least $125 million to consumers who the company wrongly pressured to pay credit card bills. Other retailers also apparently adopted the tactic, Weber said.

Sears pressured once-bankrupt debtors to sign agreements to continue to pay their credit card debts to the company, according to court documents. The Hoffman Estates, Illin.-based retailer then failed to file the agreements with bankruptcy courts as is required by law. So in some cases it continued trying to collect debts wiped out by the courts.
The practice, which dated back to at least 1985, was first brought to light in a U.S. Bankruptcy Court in Boston.

"I think it sends a definite signal that this kind of action will not be tolerated," said John Roddy, a lawyer for plaintiffs in three class-action lawsuits against Sears, the nation's second-largest retailer.
"We believe this will set the model for agreements we hope to reach in those other cases."
Roddy represents plaintiffs in similar suits against the Lechmere department store chain, owned by Montgomery Ward Holding Corp., and Filene's, owned by May Department Stores Co.
"We allege that it's engaged in systematically by May and by Ward," he said. "We believe it's across the board in terms of all the May affiliates. We just don't have the numbers yet."
May Department Stores also owns Lord & Taylor, Foley's, Hecht's, Kaufmann's and other department store chains.
Officials at May and Montgomery Ward did not return phone calls seeking comment.

Weber declined to say what retailers have been targeted. He said the states' investigation was preliminary and was based on the probe against Sears. "Now we've been through this type of investigation and know what to look for," he said.
The Justice Department also has been investigating Sears but a prosecutor in Boston declined to comment if other retailers were also under investigation.

Financial analysts said other retailers were far less active and less successful at seeking the so-called reaffirmation agreements with consumers than Sears, which has the largest credit card business among U.S. retailers.

Since Sears sells a lot of refrigerators, washing machines and other big-ticket items, its shoppers often had higher credit card balances, prompting the retailer to bring greater pressure for repayment, they said.

"The proportion of big-ticket items is much less at a Filene's than at Sears," said Joseph Ronning at Brown Brothers Harriman. "Sears used the fact that they had a security interest in the item as a lever to get people to go along with the reaffirmations."
Sears stock rose $1 to $49.875 on the New York Stock Exchange in late trading.
